they're reading copy that someone else has written to be as flashy and unoffensive as possible.

Here's a good article from Livescience.com. Basically, it comes down to three things.

  • Removing any regional accent from their speech to appeal to a broader audience
  • Pronouncing every letter in each word spoken
  • Emulating other news broadcasters

My pick for best quote from the article

To get a job somewhere you have to sound literally like you're from nowhere

It's called "having authority" - and it's a really old approach. You can hear it on early radio news from the 1920's, it reached a peak during WW2 in newsreels, and you find its child...fake excitement...all over documentaries.

One explanation is that people get used to hearing the vocal style, and they 'tune in' more readily to understand the words because the tone and approach signal "This is important information". The argument is, if you just talk in ordinary tones no one will pay attention. Sad, if true. But unfortunately, pretty likely, since the style has lasted many years and shows no sign of going away.

Incidentally, people like police and firemen take courses in "the commanding voice", so as to control people better at emergency scenes. i.e., someone bending over a heart attack victim doesn't turn to you and say quietly, "Would you mind calling 911?" They yell, and it works.

tl,dr: If you aren't frightened/excited by the sound of "authority", you won't pay attention.

They practice a lot to speak that way.

It's a clear, metered way of speaking in order to be as easy to understand as possible while covering all the news within the allotted time they have. They're also speaking into the same type of mics, in similar conditions, with similar levels in audio. It's not super difficult to learn but takes a lot of practice to do consistently.

This is a very American thing. I'm very much annoyed by it as well. They're doing it because American media are highly sensational, where viewer count is more important than journalistic professionalism.
Related: Jay Jackson's satirical take on news reporter's speech as Perd Hapley (of Parks and Rec fame). He does thisso well.
